chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Fed at the Center

lessons.title: Fed Balance Sheet Mechanics: QE, QT, and the Plumbing

body.text: Quantitative easing and quantitative tightening are not "printing money" or "shrinking the balance sheet" in any loose sense. They are precise operations in bank reserves, and the plumbing underneath, repo markets, SOFR, the reserve floor, is where liquidity stress actually shows up first, often before anyone is talking about it.

children.text: Chapter 1 introduced net liquidity as Fed Balance Sheet minus TGA minus RRP. This chapter opens up the first term in that formula. Understanding exactly how the Fed balance sheet expands and contracts, and where the mechanical stress points sit, is what lets you read a QE or QT announcement for what it actually does to markets, rather than reacting to the headline.
QE Is an Asset Swap, Not Printing Cash

When the Fed runs quantitative easing, it buys Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, typically from primary dealers, through open market operations. The Fed pays for these securities not with physical cash but by crediting the reserve account that the dealer's bank holds at the Fed. The dealer's bank ends up holding more reserves (a claim on the Fed) instead of holding a bond (a claim on the US Treasury or a mortgage pool). Nothing physical is printed. The Fed's balance sheet grows on both sides at once: securities held go up on the asset side, and reserves go up on the liability side.

body.caption: The Fed's Simplified Balance Sheet: Before and After a Round of QE

children.text: QT Is the Mirror Image, Mostly by Attrition

Quantitative tightening shrinks the balance sheet mainly through passive runoff rather than active selling. As Treasuries and MBS on the Fed's books mature or get repaid, the Fed simply chooses not to reinvest the proceeds, up to a monthly cap. Reserves fall as a mirror image of securities falling. Outright sales of securities are a second, more aggressive tool, but the Fed has relied almost entirely on passive runoff in the QT cycles run so far, because runoff is easier to calibrate without directly moving bond prices through visible selling.

body.label: 2022 QT Pace, at Full Speed
body.context: Made up of up to $60 billion in Treasuries and $35 billion in MBS runoff per month, phased in from mid-2022. The Fed later slowed this pace in 2024. Always check the FOMC's current balance sheet policy statement for the live cap.

body.text: Reserves are not spread evenly across the banking system, and demand for reserves is not perfectly stable either. The Fed's own framework distinguishes "abundant" reserves from "ample" reserves from "scarce" reserves. QT is meant to stop well before scarce territory, but because nobody can see the exact ample-to-scarce boundary in real time, QT runs the risk of draining reserves faster than the system can comfortably absorb, and finding out only when a funding market breaks.

children.text: Case Study: The September 2019 Repo Spike

body.title: How a Plumbing Problem Became a Market Event

events.title: The First Modern QT Cycle
events.description: The Fed runs balance sheet runoff for the first time since the QE era began, gradually draining reserves without a clear real-time signal of how close the system was to the "ample" reserves floor.

events.title: Overnight Repo Rates Spike
events.description: A combination of corporate tax payment outflows and a large Treasury settlement drained cash from the banking system at the same time reserves were already thin from QT. Overnight repo rates spiked as high as the high single digits intraday, well above the Fed's target range, and SOFR printed sharply higher that day.

events.title: The Fed Steps In
events.description: The Fed began daily and term repo operations to add reserves and calm the market, and restarted outright purchases of Treasury bills, describing the move explicitly as reserve management rather than a new round of QE.

events.title: The Standing Repo Facility Is Established
events.description: The Fed creates a permanent Standing Repo Facility (SRF), letting eligible institutions borrow reserves against Treasuries and other high-quality collateral on demand, explicitly built to prevent a repeat of the September 2019 spike.

body.text: The repo rate figures above are widely reported approximations from September 2019 coverage, used to illustrate the scale of the spike, not to be quoted as precise data.

children.text: The Three Rates That Define the Plumbing

body.caption: The Rates Professionals Watch to Read the Plumbing

cells: Rate the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed
Acts as the floor of the Fed's target range, anchoring short-term rates
Rate on overnight loans collateralized by Treasuries in the repo market
The Fed's preferred benchmark for the plumbing; a spike here signals reserve or collateral stress
Rate on unsecured overnight loans between banks
The Fed's traditional policy rate benchmark, sitting inside the IORB-to-SRF corridor

children.text: India has its own version of this plumbing, on a domestic scale. The RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) uses the repo and reverse repo rates to inject or absorb cash from the banking system daily, the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) lets banks park surplus cash with the RBI without collateral, and Variable Rate Repo and Reverse Repo (VRR/VRRR) auctions fine-tune liquidity at market-determined rates rather than a fixed rate. The logic is the same as the Fed's corridor: set a floor and a ceiling, and use daily operations to keep the actual overnight rate inside it. A professional who understands the Fed's IORB-SOFR-SRF corridor already has the mental model needed to read the RBI's own liquidity operations.

body.title: QE vs QT, Side by Side

columns.label: Quantitative Easing (QE)
points: Fed buys Treasuries and MBS, crediting dealer banks' reserve accounts
Balance sheet assets and reserves both rise together
Pushes longer-term yields lower and generally supports risk assets, including Nifty and other EM equities via looser global dollar liquidity

columns.label: Quantitative Tightening (QT)
points: Fed lets maturing securities run off without reinvesting, up to a monthly cap
Balance sheet assets and reserves both fall together
Tends to push yields and the dollar higher, and has historically coincided with FPI outflow pressure on the NSE and BSE

body.title: Reading a Repo Spike
body.scenario: It is September 2019. Reserves in the US banking system have been shrinking gradually for about two years as the Fed runs QT. On a single day, corporate tax payments and a large Treasury settlement both drain cash from the system at once. Overnight repo rates spike sharply above the Fed's target range.
body.prompt: Why did a temporary cash drain cause such an outsized spike in repo rates, when the Fed's balance sheet was still far larger than it had been before the 2008 crisis?
body.modelAnswer: The size of the balance sheet relative to its pre-2008 history is not what matters; what matters is how close reserves are to the "ample" threshold at that specific moment. Two years of QT had gradually drained reserves closer to that threshold without an obvious real-time warning sign. When tax payments and a Treasury settlement pulled cash out on the same day, the system had too little spare capacity to absorb the shock smoothly, and repo rates spiked because there was not enough reserve cushion left to meet the sudden spike in demand for cash. This is precisely why the Fed later built the Standing Repo Facility: to remove the need for banks to guess how much cushion is left.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What actually happens on the Fed's balance sheet when it conducts quantitative easing?
options: The Fed prints physical currency and distributes it to banks
The Fed buys securities and credits the seller's bank with new reserves, growing both sides of its balance sheet
The Fed lowers the reserve requirement for commercial banks
The Fed transfers money directly from the TGA into the stock market
body.explanation: QE is an asset swap: the Fed buys securities and pays by crediting reserves to the seller's bank. Securities held (an asset) and reserves (a liability) both rise together. No physical currency is printed as part of this process.

points: QE is an asset swap: the Fed buys securities and credits dealer banks with new reserves, growing both sides of its balance sheet together.
QT mostly works through passive runoff, letting maturing securities roll off without reinvestment up to a monthly cap, rather than active selling.
Reserves are not evenly distributed, and the boundary between "ample" and "scarce" reserves is not visible in real time, which is what made the September 2019 repo spike possible late in a QT cycle.
IORB, SOFR, and EFFR are the three rates that define the Fed's operating corridor, and a spike in SOFR specifically signals funding or collateral stress in the plumbing.
The RBI runs an analogous corridor domestically through the LAF, SDF, and VRR/VRRR operations, so the Fed's plumbing logic transfers directly to reading RBI liquidity operations.
